expansion:
Aqueous flare and cells are the correct sign of activity because the lecture lists them as the defining clinical sign of anterior uveitis on its own signs slide: “SLIDE 16 — Anterior uveitis: Signs — cells, flare and hypopyon,” printed as “Anterior chamber: Cells & flare ± hypopyon” (L13,14, slide 16). This woman's story of recurrent joint pain with recurrent attacks of pain, redness and dropped vision in one eye is a recurrent anterior uveitis, most plausibly linked to a seronegative or connective-tissue arthropathy, and the presence of protein (flare) and inflammatory cells in the aqueous is what tells the examiner the process is currently active rather than quiescent, because active inflammatory exudation is what produces them.

Festooned pupil, option A, is not listed among the lecture's active signs; a festooned or irregularly scalloped pupil margin is the visible result of posterior synechiae, which the lecture places among the sequelae and complications of uveitis rather than among the signs of current activity (L13,14, slide 18 area, "Sequelae and complications — Posterior synechiae"). A festooned pupil therefore reflects damage already done by a past attack, not proof that inflammation is happening now.

Pigmented KPs, option C, are keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium; the lecture lists them as a sign, but old, pigmented ("mutton-fat" type when granulomatous, or simply pigmented and inactive) KPs indicate a healed or chronic low-grade process rather than fresh activity, unlike fine white cells actively deposited during an acute flare — pigmentation implies the deposit has been present long enough to become pigmented, which argues for a resolving rather than an acutely active process (not taken from the course material for the pigmentation-implies-inactivity inference specifically, though KPs themselves are on the lecture's signs slide).

Patches of iris atrophy, option D, are a structural scar left behind after inflammation has damaged the iris stroma; like the festooned pupil, this is a sequela of past uveitis rather than a marker of an inflammatory episode happening at the time of examination, so it cannot be used to certify current activity.
objective: Identify aqueous flare and cells as the clinical sign of active anterior uveitis, as distinct from its structural sequelae
